c1-m1.summary: The user is seeking information about pet care.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm looking for some general information on pets. Do you have any resources on pet care?
Assistant: Yes, I do. I can provide information on nutrition, health, and behavior for various types of pets. What type of pet are you interested in learning about?
User: I have a dog, and I'm concerned about its health. What are some common health issues in dogs?
Assistant: Dogs can be prone to various health issues, such as hip dysplasia, allergies, and obesity. It's also important to monitor their mental health and watch for signs of anxiety or stress. How old is your dog?
User: My dog is about 5 years old. It's been acting strangely lately, and I'm not sure what's wrong. Can you tell me about some possible causes of strange behavior in dogs?
Assistant: At 5 years old, your dog is considered an adult, and strange behavior can be caused by a variety of factors, including medical issues, changes in environment, or even boredom. Can you describe the strange behavior you've observed in your dog?
User: It's been having trouble walking and seems to be losing its balance. It also has seizures sometimes. I'm worried that it might be something serious.
Assistant: I understand your concern. The symptoms you've described could be indicative of a neurological disorder. Has your dog been diagnosed with any medical conditions, or have you consulted a veterinarian about its symptoms?
User: Not yet, I'm trying to gather more information before taking it to the vet. Can you tell me more about neurological disorders in dogs?
Assistant: Neurological disorders in dogs can be caused by various factors, such as genetics, infections, or injuries. Some common neurological disorders in dogs include epilepsy, degenerative myelopathy, and peripheral neuropathy. It's essential to consult a veterinarian to determine the cause of your dog's symptoms and develop a treatment plan.
User: That's really helpful information. What are some signs that a dog's neurological disorder is progressing, and what can be done to manage its symptoms?
Assistant: Signs of progression may include increased frequency or severity of seizures, worsening balance or coordination, and changes in behavior or cognitive function. Managing symptoms may involve medication, physical therapy, or lifestyle changes, such as providing a safe and comfortable living space. Your veterinarian can work with you to develop a treatment plan tailored to your dog's specific needs.
User: Are there any alternative or holistic approaches that can help alleviate my dog's symptoms?
Assistant: Some alternative approaches, such as acupuncture, massage, or chiropractic care, may help alleviate symptoms and improve your dog's quality of life. However, it's essential to consult with a veterinarian before pursuing any alternative therapies to ensure they won't interact with conventional treatments or worsen your dog's condition.
User: How can I best support my dog during this time, and what can I do to make it more comfortable?
Assistant: Providing a comfortable and stress-free environment is crucial. You can make adjustments to your dog's living space, such as removing tripping hazards, providing a comfortable place to rest, and ensuring easy access to food, water, and medication. Additionally, maintaining a regular routine and spending quality time with your dog can help reduce stress and promote a sense of well-being.
User: Last question: What are the most important things to discuss with my veterinarian during our upcoming appointment?
Assistant: Be sure to discuss your dog's symptoms, medical history, and any changes you've observed. Ask about the diagnosis, treatment options, and prognosis. It's also essential to ask about any lifestyle changes or adjustments you can make to support your dog's health and well-being. Write down any questions or concerns you have, so you don't forget to address them during the appointment.
User: Hi, I'm feeling really overwhelmed today. I don't know what to do.
Assistant: I'm here to help. Can you tell me a little bit more about what's going on? What's causing you to feel overwhelmed?
User: It's just been a really tough week. I've been running around nonstop and I feel like I'm not getting anything done.
Assistant: I understand. It sounds like you're feeling a bit burnt out. Have you taken any time for yourself lately to relax and recharge?
User: Honestly, no. I don't think I've had a free moment in days. And to make matters worse, I just got some news that's making things even harder.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that. It sounds like things are really piling up on you. Can you tell me more about this news you just got?
User: It's just... a family member is dealing with some health issues and I need to be there for them.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that. Dealing with a loved one's health issues can be really tough. Are they okay? What's going on with their health?
User: They've been hospitalized, so I need to spend some time at the hospital with them.
Assistant: I'm here for you. That can be really challenging. How are you feeling about the hospitalization? Are you getting the support you need?
User: To be honest, I'm feeling really anxious about it. I don't know what to expect or how long they'll be in the hospital.
Assistant: That's completely understandable. It's natural to feel anxious in this situation. Have you talked to the hospital staff about your family member's condition and what you can expect?
User: Yeah, I've talked to the doctors and nurses, but I still feel like I'm in the dark about a lot of things.
Assistant: It might be helpful to ask them to explain things in more detail or to provide you with regular updates on your family member's condition. Would you like some help brainstorming questions to ask them?
User: That would actually be really helpful. I feel like I don't know what to ask or who to ask.
Assistant: Okay, I can help you with that. I can also provide some general information about hospital procedures and what to expect. Would you like that?

c9-m1.summary: The user experienced a scary experience while hiking near a cliff.
c9-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Doctor, I had a scary experience recently. I was out hiking and almost fell off a cliff.
Assistant: That sounds terrifying. Are you okay?
User: Yes, thankfully I was able to step back in time.
Assistant: I'm glad you avoided disaster. Did you experience any injuries or symptoms after the incident?
User: No, I'm physically fine, but it was a wake-up call for me to be more cautious in the future.
Assistant: That's a good mindset to have. Speaking of caution, how have you been managing your neurological disorder?
User: I've been following the treatment plan you recommended, and my symptoms have improved significantly. Thank you for your help and expertise.
Assistant: I'm glad to hear that. Let's continue to monitor your progress and adjust the treatment plan if necessary. Remember to also prioritize your mental health and overall well-being as you navigate through these health challenges.
User: Doctor, I had a scary experience recently. I was walking near the edge of a cliff and almost fell over. I'm still shaken up by it.
Assistant: That sounds incredibly frightening. I'm glad you were able to step back in time and avoid disaster. Have you experienced anything like this before?
User: Not to this extent. It's made me realize how important it is to be aware of my surroundings and take steps to keep myself safe.
Assistant: Absolutely. It's important for anyone with a neurological disorder to take extra precautions to ensure their safety. Have you noticed any improvement in your symptoms since we last spoke?
User: Yes, actually. The treatment you prescribed has been helping a lot. I feel like I have more control over my movements and my quality of life has improved.
Assistant: That's wonderful to hear. Remember that it's important to continue following your treatment plan and to communicate with me if you experience any changes or new symptoms.
User: I will. Thank you for your guidance, Doctor. I really appreciate your help in managing my condition.
Assistant: You're welcome, Patient. We're in this together and I'll do everything I can to support you on your journey to better health.

c11-m1.summary: The user is seeking medical assistance for a rare neurological disorder.
c11-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Thank you for seeing me today, Doctor. I'm really hopeful that you can help me manage my rare neurological disorder.
Assistant: Of course, it's my pleasure to help. Can you tell me a bit more about your symptoms and how they've been affecting you?
User: Well, I've been experiencing a lot of muscle weakness, fatigue and tremors. It's been very difficult to carry out daily tasks, and I'm feeling quite discouraged.
Assistant: I understand how difficult that must be. Based on what you've told me, I recommend a treatment plan that includes physical therapy, medication and dietary changes. How does that sound to you?
User: That sounds great. I'm willing to do whatever it takes to get better.
Assistant: Excellent. We'll start you on medication to help manage your symptoms, and I'll refer you to a physical therapist who specializes in neurological disorders. We'll also work with a nutritionist to make sure you're eating a healthy diet that promotes brain health.
User: That all sounds very comprehensive. I'm really grateful for your help, Doctor.
Assistant: It's my pleasure, Patient. We'll work together to help you manage your symptoms and improve your quality of life. And if you have any concerns along the way, don't hesitate to reach out to me.
User: Doctor, I'm so excited to be in the city for the first time! There's so much to see and explore.
Assistant: That's great to hear! It's always good to experience new things and broaden your horizons. Just make sure to pace yourself and take breaks if you get tired.
User: Yes, I'm trying to take it slow and not overdo it. But I just can't believe the size of some of these skyscrapers!
Assistant: It's definitely a different world compared to the quiet countryside where you're from. How's your neurological disorder been treating you lately?
User: Thankfully, my symptoms have been under control with the medication and therapy we discussed during our last visit. I'm really grateful for the progress we've made.
Assistant: That's fantastic to hear! Remember to keep up with your treatment plan and let me know if there are any changes in your symptoms. Enjoy the rest of your time in the city!

User: Given the text: Welcome to the Marcus Neuroscience Institute at Boca Raton Regional Hospital, an innovative nexus for neurologic and neurosurgical care. This new 57,000-square-foot facility houses a 20-bed Neuro Intensive Care and Step-Down Unit, four dedicated operating rooms — including one equipped with intraoperative MRI and two with intraoperative CT capability — and a biplane angiography suite, a crucial component in the diagnosis and care of neurological conditions.
The Institute was created out of a lead $25 million grant from the Marcus Foundation and was initiated by Billi and Bernie Marcus, former CEO of The Home Depot.
The institute is staffed by a team of clinicians highly trained in all facets of the neurosciences, including stroke, movement disorders, neuro-oncology, epilepsy, memory disorders, Alzheimer’s disease, multiple sclerosis and spinal conditions. The medical staff also includes neurointensivists, physicians who are specifically trained in neurocritical care. Along with having extensive knowledge about treating neurological injuries, neurointensivists assume responsibility for other areas of care in the ICU that may have otherwise been provided by specialists. This includes cardiology, endocrinology, infectious disease and pulmonary medicine.
Each patient room at the Marcus Neuroscience Institute is private and equipped with special monitoring capabilities that provide vital information on both a patient’s neurological and cardiovascular functions. Rooms also feature an abundance of natural lighting and an antechamber where family members can stay during the patient’s hospitalization, as both of these factors have been shown to positively influence recovery in neurological conditions.
Patients also benefit from the Institute’s synergistic relationship with Boca Regional’s Eugene M. & Christine E. Lynn Cancer Institute (LCI), offering patients with neurologic malignancies the most advanced radiation and medical oncology therapies available in LCI’s renowned and award-winning facility. The combination of LCI and the Marcus Neuroscience Institute makes for a tandem of facilities, programs and services that is among the finest in the nation.
The creation of the Marcus Neuroscience Institute represents a watershed moment in the advancement of the neurosciences in Florida and beyond.
For more information, call 561.955.4600.

User: What are the potential implications of this research for cell replacement therapies in treating neurological diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's?
Generate according to: Neurons genetically rendered hyperactive (red) survive better than normal neurons (green). Traces at bottom of the image show the electrical activity of genetically-manipulated neurons (red trace) and normal neurons (green trace).
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. — MIT neuroscientists have discovered that when it comes to new neurons in the adult brain, the squeakiest wheels get the grease.
Neuronal survival is a key component to the success of cell replacement therapies in the brain. Current therapies have hit a roadblock because the vast majority of grafted cells do not survive and do not integrate into adult brain circuits. “Our discovery of a survival-determining mechanism in new neurons is likely to have a significant influence on such treatments,” said Lois, an assistant professor of neuroscience.
In addition, the observation that the “noisiest” neurons have a survival advantage helps explain the prevalence of epilepsy, in which some neurons become hyperactive and fire in an uncontrollable fashion. “Our work suggests that any perturbation that increases the activity of neurons will enhance the likelihood of their survival. Thus, during childhood, when many neurons are still being added to the brain, it is likely that neurons that become pathologically hyperactive will be preferentially selected for survival, and these abnormal neurons will be the trigger for epilepsy,” Lois said.
HOW THEY DID IT: To investigate whether activity levels—and the source and pattern of activity — are crucial in governing whether an individual new neuron survives or dies, the researchers used new technology to genetically enhance or dampen the electrical excitability of single adult-generated neurons. An important technological advance, the methods used in this study allow for single-cell genetic manipulation of electrical activity in living animals.
NEXT STEPS: Investigating the molecular signals launched by neuronal activity will potentially lead to new drugs that bolster the survival of new neurons. These drugs could be used to increase the efficacy of treatments that depend on grafting stem cell-derived neurons into the adult brain to treat neurological diseases such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.
SOURCE: “Genetically increased cell-intrinsic excitability enhances neuronal integration into adult brain circuits,” by Chiawei Lin, Shuyin Sim, Masayoshi Okada, Alice Ainsworth, Wolfgang Kelsch and Carlos Lois in Neuron, published Jan. 14, 2010.
FUNDING: The work was funded by the National lnstitutes of Health.
Assistant: The research suggests that enhancing the activity levels of newly generated neurons could improve their survival and integration into adult brain circuits. This finding could have significant implications for cell replacement therapies in treating neurological diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, which rely on grafting stem cell-derived neurons into the adult brain. By investigating the molecular signals launched by neuronal activity, new drugs could be developed to bolster the survival of new neurons, increasing the efficacy of these treatments. Additionally, the study helps explain the prevalence of epilepsy and suggests that any perturbation that increases the activity of neurons will enhance the likelihood of their survival.

Assistant: The article doesn't provide specific details on the molecular signals launched by neuronal activity. However, the article suggests that investigating these signals could potentially lead to the development of new drugs that enhance the survival of new neurons. It's possible that further research in this area may identify specific molecular mechanisms involved in neuronal survival and integration, which could be targeted for therapeutic development.
User: Can you explain how the researchers genetically enhanced or dampened the electrical excitability of single adult-generated neurons?
Assistant: The researchers used a new technology to genetically enhance or dampen the electrical excitability of single adult-generated neurons. They used viral vectors to deliver genes to the neurons, allowing them to manipulate the neurons' electrical activity. Specifically, the researchers used genes that encoded for two different ion channels: one channel that would increase the electrical activity of the neuron, and one channel that would decrease it. By using these viral vectors to selectively express these genes in single neurons, the researchers were able to enhance or dampen the electrical activity of individual neurons in living animals. This allowed them to investigate whether activity levels are crucial in governing whether a new neuron survives or dies.

User: How does age play a role in the onset and severity of symptoms in hereditary neurological disorders?
Assistant: Age can play a significant role in the onset and severity of symptoms in hereditary neurological disorders. Certain disorders have a specific age of onset, such as Huntington's disease, which typically appears in adulthood between the ages of 30 and 50. However, many other disorders can have a wide range of age onset and severity.

In some cases, symptoms may appear early in life and progress rapidly, such as in infantile or childhood-onset forms of disorders like Tay-Sachs disease or Batten disease. Alternatively, some neurological disorders may have a late onset, usually after age 60, resulting in milder symptoms, such as late-onset Alzheimer's disease.

The severity of symptoms can also vary depending on the age of onset. An individual with an early onset of a hereditary neurological disorder is likely to experience more aggressive symptoms compared to a person with a later onset of the same disorder. For example, early onset Parkinson's disease typically progresses faster and has a greater impact on a person's quality of life than later onset Parkinson's disease.

Overall, the relationship between age and the onset and severity of symptoms in hereditary neurological disorders is complex and varies between different disorders. Still, age is a crucial factor to consider, both in disease progression and treatment strategies.
User: Can lifestyle factors like diet and exercise affect the onset and severity of symptoms in hereditary neurological disorders?
Assistant: Yes, lifestyle factors like diet and exercise can influence the onset and severity of symptoms in some hereditary neurological disorders. Research has shown that a healthy lifestyle may reduce the risk of developing some diseases or slow their progression in people who already have the condition.

In terms of diet, some studies have suggested that a Mediterranean-style diet may be beneficial in managing symptoms of neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease. The diet is rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, and healthy fats, and it has been shown to reduce inflammation in the body, which can be beneficial for those with neurodegenerative disorders.

Exercise has also been shown to be beneficial in managing symptoms of some neurological disorders. Physical activity can improve cardiovascular health, which can be helpful in reducing the risk of developing some disorders. Studies have also shown that moderate exercise may improve cognitive function in people with neurological disorders like Alzheimer's disease and increase mobility in those with Parkinson's disease.

Overall, while lifestyle factors like diet and exercise may not directly prevent or cure hereditary neurological disorders, they can play a role in managing symptoms and improving overall quality of life for those affected by these conditions.
User: Are there any particular foods or exercises that should be avoided in hereditary neurological disorders?
Assistant: It depends on the specific hereditary neurological disorder in question, as each disorder has its unique set of symptoms and dietary recommendations.

For example, some individuals with Huntington's disease may experience difficulty with swallowing and may need to follow a soft or pureed food diet. They may also need to avoid foods that are difficult to chew, such as nuts, seeds, and raw vegetables.

In neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson's disease, some individuals may experience gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation, which may require the inclusion of high-fiber foods in their diet. However, some high-fiber foods like beans and legumes may sometimes exacerbate bloating and gas in some individuals.

As for exercise, it is essential to consult a healthcare provider, as some individuals with certain neurological disorders may have limited mobility or other issues that can be made worse by particular exercises.

In general, a healthy, balanced diet that is rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein sources is ideal for most people, including those with hereditary neurological disorders. Similarly, moderate exercise, such as swimming, walking or cycling, can offer benefits for a variety of neurological disorders. However, it is crucial to work with healthcare professionals to develop personalized dietary and exercise plans that are tailored to individual needs and abilities.

User: Can you provide a link to donate to research into INAD?
Generate according to: Countless little pieces of confetti will go flying tomorrow for one particular Yinnar South teenager.
Fifteen-year-old Nessa Williames' mother Sue has organised for 125 kids to get together under a disco ball and enjoy the light, colour and sounds.
"Nessa loves colours and she loves discos and when I found out she was losing her sight I went 'I need to do something really special for her'," Ms Williames said.
The family recently heard a diagnosis for Nessa's condition which has been degenerative since the age of about three and resulted in years of "often invasive" testing.
After a full genome sequence, they discovered with both "shock" and "relief" that Nessa had a very rare neurological disorder called infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.
Ms Williames only knows of two other people in Australia with the condition.
"She was really quite bright. The signature of this disease is children lose everything they had. They gain these milestones then they lose them again," Ms Williames said.
Nessa has the atypical form of the condition, which Ms Williames said meant she was likely to live longer than if she had the classic form, but she was still "on borrowed time".
Last Christmas Nessa started having absent seizures and her family started suspecting her vision was failing.
Then testing revealed optic nerve atrophy, confirming Nessa was losing her eyesight.
Ms Williames said she had dealt with her daughter's condition for 12 years, but the extent of her degeneration made it now "so hard".
"The hardest thing is going into shops now at Christmas because there's nothing I can buy Nessa," she said.

Assistant: Sorry to hear that. Would you like to talk about what's going on and maybe I can help?
User: Yeah, I just feel really overwhelmed. I've got a lot of responsibilities and sometimes it feels like everything is piling up on me.
Assistant: It sounds like you're feeling a bit burnt out. Can you tell me more about these responsibilities? Maybe we can break them down and find ways to make them more manageable.
User: Well, I take care of my home, my family... and my pets. It's just a lot to handle sometimes.
Assistant: It sounds like you have a lot of dependents relying on you. That can be really tough. How are your pets doing, by the way?
User: Actually, that's part of why I'm stressed out. One of them isn't doing very well, and I'm not sure what to do.
Assistant: Oh no, sorry to hear that. What's going on with your pet? Is it a recent development or something that's been ongoing?
User: It's been going on for a few days now. I've noticed some changes in their behavior and they seem to be in some discomfort. I'm not sure what's causing it or how to make it better.
Assistant: That must be really worrying for you. Have you considered taking your pet to see a vet? They would be able to assess the situation and provide some guidance on what to do next.
User: Yeah, that's a good idea. I actually have an appointment scheduled for later today, but I'm not sure what to expect or what questions to ask.
Assistant: That's great that you have an appointment! It's always a good idea to write down any questions or concerns you have beforehand so you don't forget to ask them. What are some of the specific changes you've noticed in your pet's behavior?
User: Well, they've been acting really lethargic and haven't been eating as much as usual. They also seem to be having some trouble moving around.
Assistant: Those are definitely concerning symptoms. It's possible that your pet is experiencing some kind of pain or discomfort that's causing them to behave this way. The vet should be able to help you get to the bottom of it. Do you have any idea what might have caused this sudden change?
User: No, I'm not really sure. That's part of why I'm so worried. I feel like I've been taking good care of them, but maybe there's something I've missed.
Assistant: It's understandable to feel that way, but it's unlikely that you've done anything wrong. Sometimes pets just get sick or injured, and it's not always preventable. The important thing is that you're taking action now and seeking help. I'm sure the vet will be able to help you figure out what's going on and find a way to make your pet feel better.
User: Hi, I'm not feeling too great today. I was thinking of going out for a walk, but I don't know if that's a good idea.
Assistant: Sorry to hear that you're not feeling well. What's going on? Do you have any symptoms that might make it difficult for you to go for a walk?
User: Yeah, my head is killing me and my sinuses are acting up. I just feel really congested and stuffy.
Assistant: That doesn't sound fun. Have you tried taking any medication to help alleviate your symptoms?
User: Yeah, I've taken some over-the-counter stuff, but it's not really helping. I'm starting to feel like I'm stuck in a rut.
Assistant: It can be really frustrating when you're not feeling well and nothing seems to be helping. Have you considered talking to a doctor about your symptoms?
User: Yeah, I think that's a good idea. I just wish I could get out of the house and get some fresh air. Being cooped up is making me feel worse.
Assistant: Sometimes, getting out and getting some fresh air can really help. But if you're not feeling up to it, maybe we can brainstorm some other ways to make you feel more comfortable at home.
User: Yeah, that sounds good. I just feel so... stuck. I hate being stuck in the house all day.
Assistant: It can be really tough to feel like you're losing a day to illness. But taking care of yourself is important. Can you tell me more about what's going on with your sinuses? Is this a recurring issue for you?
User: Yeah... I think I might have a severe allergy or sinus infection. It's making it really hard for me to breathe and it's painful.
Assistant: That sounds really tough. If you have a severe allergy or sinus infection, it's no wonder you're not feeling well enough to leave the house. Have you talked to a doctor about getting some stronger medication or treatment?
User: Not yet, but I think I need to. I'm just not sure how to manage my symptoms in the meantime.
Assistant: Okay, well, let's start with some basics. Have you tried using a humidifier or a saline nasal spray to help loosen up some of that congestion?
User: Yeah, I have a humidifier, but I haven't been using it as much as I should. And I don't have a saline nasal spray. Maybe I'll try that.
Assistant: That's a good idea. I can also give you some general tips on how to manage your symptoms until you can see a doctor. Would you like that?

c25-m1.summary: The user is a cat lover.
c25-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I was just thinking about my family and all the exciting things happening this year. How about you, do you get to be a part of any fun events or celebrations?
Assistant: I don't have personal experiences, but I love hearing about yours! It sounds like you have some exciting things to look forward to. Are you attending any weddings or graduations?
User: Actually, yes, my sister's getting married soon. It's been a long time coming, and we're all super excited. The whole family's really looking forward to it.
Assistant: That's wonderful! Sisters' weddings can be such a special time. Are you involved in the planning process at all, or is that mostly your sister's domain?
User: Yeah, I'm helping out a bit here and there. We're a pretty close-knit family, so everyone's pitching in. I'm actually supposed to be in the rehearsal, which should be fun.
Assistant: That sounds great! Being part of the rehearsal can be a fantastic experience. When is the rehearsal scheduled, do you know the exact dates yet?
User: Yeah, I do. It's about two weeks from now. We're still finalizing a few details, but I'm getting a bit worried about something else.
Assistant: Oh? What's on your mind? Hopefully, it's nothing too serious.
User: Well, as I prepare for my sister's wedding, I need to ensure my dog's regular vet check-ups don't clash with the rehearsal schedule. I completely forgot that my dog has an appointment around the same time, and I'm not sure how to juggle both.
Assistant: Ah, that can be a challenge. But don't worry, we can figure it out. Can you tell me a bit more about your dog's vet schedule and the rehearsal timeline? Maybe we can find a way to make both work.
User: Yeah, sure. The vet appointment is actually on the same day as the rehearsal, but in the morning. The rehearsal is in the late afternoon. I'm just worried that the vet appointment might run long, or something unexpected will come up.
Assistant: Okay, that's understandable. Here's what we can do: why don't you call the vet's office and confirm the appointment time? Also, ask them about their typical wait times and if they have any flexibility in case you need to reschedule or rush the appointment.
User: That's a great idea. And what about the rehearsal? Should I let my sister know about the potential conflict?
Assistant: Yes, it's always better to communicate these things ahead of time. Let your sister know about the vet appointment and see if there's a plan B in case you're running late. You can also offer to rehearse your part beforehand, so you're not completely missing out if you do end up being late.
User: Okay, I feel a bit better now. I think I'll call the vet and my sister today to get everything sorted out.
Assistant: Sounds like a plan! And don't forget to take care of yourself during this time, too. It's great that you're thinking ahead and trying to balance everything. Your sister will appreciate it, and I'm sure your dog will be just fine.
User: Hi, I'm a huge cat lover. I've had my cat, Luna, since she was a kitten. She's such a sweetheart, but I've noticed she can get a bit anxious around new people. Have you worked with cats like that before?
Assistant: Ah, yes! Many cats can be quite particular about their social circle. I've worked with plenty of cat owners who've struggled with socialization issues. What makes you think Luna is anxious around new people? Does she exhibit any specific behaviors?
User: Well, she tends to hide under the bed or in a closet when someone new comes over. And if they try to pet her, she'll sometimes swat at their hand. It's like she's trying to protect herself. I've tried to coax her out, but it takes a while for her to warm up.
Assistant: That sounds like pretty typical behavior for a cat who's not confident around new people. It's great that you're aware of her boundaries and are trying to help her feel more comfortable. Can you tell me a bit more about Luna's personality? What's she like when it's just the two of you at home?
User: Oh, she's a total diva! She loves attention and affection from me, and she's always curling up in my lap or sleeping next to me. But like I said, when new people come over, she's a different cat altogether.
Assistant: That's hilarious! It sounds like she's got a bit of a split personality. Don't worry, it's not uncommon for cats to be more reserved around new people. It's actually a sign of intelligence and adaptability. Now, I'm curious – what's prompted you to want to work on Luna's socialization skills? Is there something specific coming up that's got you concerned?
User: Actually, yes... With the upcoming family reunion, I want to make sure Luna is comfortable around a lot of people. We're hosting it at our place, and I know it'll be chaos. I don't want her to be stressed out the whole time.
Assistant: Ah, I see! A big family reunion can be overwhelming for anyone, let alone a sensitive cat like Luna. Okay, let's get to work on a plan to help her feel more confident and calm around all those new people. One thing we can try is gradual exposure to new people and environments. We can start by having a few friends over for small gatherings and rewarding Luna with treats and praise when she behaves calmly.
User: That sounds like a great idea! But what if she still gets overwhelmed? I don't want her to feel like she's being forced to interact if she's not comfortable.
Assistant: Absolutely, we need to respect her boundaries. One thing we can do is set up a few "safe zones" around the house where Luna can retreat if she's feeling overwhelmed. This could be a quiet room or a high perch where she can observe from a distance. We can also make sure to provide plenty of hiding spots and vertical space for her to climb and escape if needed.
User: Okay, that makes sense. What about during the actual reunion? How can I make sure she's not too stressed out?
Assistant: Well, one thing we can do is create a "cat agility course" of sorts to distract her from all the commotion. We can set up tunnels, scratching posts, and toys to keep her occupied and engaged. You can also try providing some calming aids like pheromone diffusers or calming treats to help her relax.
User: Hmm, I like the idea of the agility course. But what about when people want to pet her or interact with her? How can I politely tell them to back off if she's not in the mood?
Assistant: Ah, that's a great question! It's totally fine to set boundaries and advocate for Luna's needs. You can simply say something like, "Hey, Luna's feeling a bit overwhelmed right now, so let's give her some space." Or, "She's not really in the mood for pets right now, but you can try offering her a treat instead." Remember, it's okay to prioritize Luna's needs and comfort level – after all, she's a member of the family too!

Question/Instruction: Can you share a personal experience you had as a cardiologist turned hospice physician, and how it influenced your decision to switch to hospice care?

Given material: We try so hard to keep thoughts of death in our subconscious minds that we miss a wonderful opportunity to have the end of life be a positive event, both for the departed and the loved ones left behind.
I recently retired from my practice of cardiology after almost 30 years. I loved this work for a very long time, and was proud to care for many people in a way that brought much appreciation from my patients and their families. But the field of medicine has changed drastically over the past 10 years or so, and I felt it was time to reconsider my own final professional chapter.
I served as the medical director for a hospice organization in Milwaukee about 10 years ago for a short time. It was decidedly unusual for a cardiologist to assume this role, as most of us in that field spend long and sometimes harrowing hours trying very hard to save and maintain lives. These are gallant fights, aided by ever more promising technical advances and procedures.
When a former colleague who practiced pulmonary medicine and critical care in the same system where I practiced cardiology called me a few months ago to tell me that he has been the medical director for a local hospice program, and needed some help as his workload had been steadily increasing, I acquiesced.
As part of my orientation, I sat in a long meeting in which the patients currently enrolled in the home hospice program were discussed. This brought back memories for me, and it felt familiar, despite a 10-year hiatus.
About 95% of hospice care is delivered in the home, which is where it should be given. Statistics show that 90% of us say that we would want to die at home, surrounded by those who love us. Unfortunately, about 70% of us die in intensive care units or nursing homes in atmospheres not at all conducive to peace and tranquility. So, culturally we have a huge gap to bridge. Hospice care is that bridge most of the time.
The time from enrollment in hospice care to death is far too short most of the time. Hospice is well-equipped to meet a wide variety of needs for both patient and family. The first priority is to alleviate suffering, both physical and emotional. Comfort is always the goal and is nearly always achieved.
A wide variety of professionals is on board for every case — doctors, nurses, pastoral care providers, social workers and volunteers work hard to understand all of the issues of each patient enrolled in this care, which is covered by Medicare with no co-pays or deductibles.
A very small number of patients receiving hospice care need to be in an inpatient facility. There are a variety of reasons for this. After attending the team meeting to discuss the home patients, my colleague walked me over to the inpatient area of the hospice. He said he wanted to introduce me, or reintroduce me, to a former patient on whom I had performed an emergency angioplasty 19 years ago as he was having a heart attack.
Carl had been admitted the afternoon before due to difficulty in controlling his pain. As we walked into his room, I noted first that he was asleep and breathing comfortably. His wife looked up with a big smile and told me immediately that she would never forget me because I had been the only doctor she had ever met who introduced himself by his first and last name, not as Dr. Somebody. She commented that Carl had spoken hundreds of times about how I had saved his life back then. Then she gave me a big hug.
I went over and put my hand on Carl's shoulder. He opened his eyes, and a big smile spread across his face. We chatted for about 10 minutes. He was very peaceful and appreciative. The other doctor then asked him if the pain regimen they had placed him on the evening before had worked out for him. Carl said that it had, indeed, and then expressed his gratitude for all of the care from all of the people at the hospice, claiming them to be like angels.
In the end, as we were preparing to leave, Carl, who had been a superb nurse in an ICU at a local hospital for his entire career, said to my colleague, "Everybody in the world ought to have the opportunity to die like this."
Hospice care is not always perfect. But the goals are always the same. Nobody should ever die alone or without their dignity. The problem in this country is that we are so busy fighting off death that we don't take time to make sure that there is plenty of time at the end for the war to be won, even though the battle against the particular disease has been lost.
Bruce C. Wilson has been a cardiologist in Milwaukee for more than 20 years and is now a hospice physician.
Assistant: As a cardiologist turned hospice physician, Bruce C. Wilson had a personal experience that influenced his decision to switch to hospice care. He served as the medical director for a hospice organization in Milwaukee about 10 years ago, and recently, when a former colleague who practiced pulmonary medicine and critical care in the same system where Wilson practiced cardiology called him for help, Wilson decided to return to hospice care. During his orientation, Wilson sat in a long meeting in which the patients currently enrolled in the home hospice program were discussed, which reminded him of his past experience in hospice care. Hospice care is the bridge between the desire to die at home and the reality of dying in an intensive care unit or nursing home. The hospice team, which includes doctors, nurses, pastoral care providers, social workers, and volunteers, work together to meet the needs of the patient and their family. While hospice care is not always perfect, the goal is always the same - to ensure that nobody dies alone or without their dignity.
User: Can you give some examples of how hospice care is able to alleviate physical and emotional suffering for patients and their families?
Assistant: Sure, here are some examples of how hospice care is able to alleviate physical and emotional suffering for patients and their families:

1. Pain management: Hospice care has a team of healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and other specialists, who are experts in relieving pain and other symptoms associated with the patient's health condition.

2. Emotional support: Hospice care provides counseling and emotional support for patients and their families, helping them cope with their emotions and fears, and providing comfort and reassurance during this difficult time.

3. Spiritual care: Hospice care also provides spiritual care for patients and their families, respecting their beliefs and values, and addressing their spiritual needs.

4. Personalized care plans: Hospice care creates individualized care plans tailored to the patient's specific needs, preferences, and goals, ensuring that the care provided is focused on the patient's comfort and quality of life.

5. Social support: Hospice care can provide social support to patients and their families, connecting them with peer support groups, bereavement counseling, and other community resources.

Overall, hospice care is a comprehensive approach that addresses the physical, emotional, and spiritual needs of patients and their families, aiming to provide comfort and dignity during the end-of-life journey.
User: Can you explain why hospice care is mostly delivered in the home and why dying at home is preferred by many people?
Assistant: Hospice care is mostly delivered in the home because it allows patients to remain in a familiar and comfortable environment surrounded by loved ones. For many individuals, being at home with family and friends provides a sense of security, belonging, and emotional support that is difficult to replicate in a hospital or long-term care facility. Dying at home also allows patients to maintain a sense of control over their lives and care, helping them make important decisions about their end-of-life wishes and personal preferences.

Dying at home is preferred by many people for a number of reasons. First, it provides a sense of comfort and familiarity that is difficult to achieve in an institutional setting. Patients are able to remain in familiar surroundings, surrounded by their belongings, pets, and family members. Second, it allows for greater autonomy and control over one's end-of-life care, giving patients the opportunity to make choices about their medical treatment and pain management. Third, it often allows for greater emotional and spiritual support, with patients and caregivers able to draw on the support of family members, friends, and local community resources.

Overall, hospice care provides an opportunity for patients to receive comprehensive, compassionate care in the comfort of their own homes. It is a way to ensure that patients are surrounded by supportive and loving individuals during one of the most challenging times of their lives.

c45-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm thinking about making a big change in my life. I'm not sure where to start.
Assistant: Hi there! It sounds like you're considering something significant. Can you tell me a bit more about what's on your mind? What kind of change are you thinking about?
User: I've been renting for a while now, and I'm starting to think about my long-term options.
Assistant: That's a great topic to explore. Renting can be a good option for flexibility, but it's natural to consider other possibilities. Are you thinking about staying in the same area or possibly moving to a new location?
User: I like where I live, so I think I'll stay in the same area. But I'm not sure what my next steps should be.
Assistant: Staying in a familiar area can make things easier. Have you thought about what your priorities are for this change? For example, are you looking for more space or a different type of living arrangement?
User: I think I'd like to have more control over my living space and maybe even build some equity.
Assistant: Those are great goals. It sounds like you might be considering buying a home. Is that something you've thought about before, or is this a new idea for you?
User: Yeah, I've thought about it a bit. But I've never actually gone through the process before. To be honest, I'm a bit overwhelmed by the idea of it all.
Assistant: Buying a home can be a complex process, especially if you're new to it. But don't worry, I'm here to help. Can you tell me a bit more about what's overwhelming you? Is it the financial aspect, the paperwork, or something else?
User: I think it's just that I've never done it before. I'm not sure where to start or what to expect. And, as I mentioned, I'm looking for my first home.
Assistant: Well, let's break it down together. As a first-time homebuyer, you'll want to start by getting pre-approved for a mortgage and understanding your budget. Then, we can discuss the different types of homes and neighborhoods that might be a good fit for you.
User: That sounds like a great plan. What's the first step in getting pre-approved for a mortgage?
Assistant: Typically, you'll want to contact a lender and provide some financial information, such as your income, credit score, and debt. They'll use this information to give you an idea of how much you can borrow and what your monthly payments might be.
User: Okay, that makes sense. And what about working with a real estate agent? Do I need to do that?
Assistant: While it's not required, working with a real estate agent can be very helpful, especially as a first-time homebuyer. They can guide you through the process, help you find homes that fit your criteria, and negotiate on your behalf. Would you like some tips on finding a good agent?
User: Hi, I'm looking for some advice on getting a loan. I've been doing some research, but I'm not sure where to start.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help you with that. Can you tell me a bit more about what you're looking for? Are you trying to get a mortgage, a personal loan, or something else?
User: I'm actually looking to get a mortgage. I've been renting for a while now, and I think it's time for me to own my own home.
Assistant: That's a big step. Congratulations on considering taking the leap. What's your current financial situation like? Do you have a steady income and a good credit score?
User: Yeah, I think so. I've been working in the same industry for a while now, and I've been trying to save up for a down payment. But I'm not sure if my income will be a problem.
Assistant: What do you mean by that? Are you self-employed or do you have a non-traditional income structure?
User: Well, I do get a base salary, but I also get bonuses and commissions. It's a bit complicated, but I'm not sure how that will affect my chances of getting a loan.
Assistant: That can make things a bit more challenging. Lenders like to see a steady, predictable income stream when evaluating creditworthiness. But it's not impossible to get a loan with a complex income structure. Can you tell me more about your bonuses and commissions? How often do you receive them, and how much do they typically add to your income?
User: Yeah, sure. I get a quarterly bonus, and it's usually around 10-20% of my base salary. And then I get commissions on top of that, which can vary depending on my performance.
Assistant: Okay, that helps to give me a better picture. In that case, we may need to look at some specialized lenders that are more accustomed to dealing with complex income structures. We may also need to provide some additional documentation to support your income claims.
User: That sounds like a good plan. I was worried that my income would be a major obstacle, but it sounds like there are some options available.
Assistant: Absolutely. It may take a bit more work, but we can definitely explore some options that will work for you. I'd be happy to help you shop around for lenders and find the best fit for your situation.
User: Great, thank you so much for your help. I feel a lot more confident now about my chances of getting a loan.
Assistant: You're welcome! I'm glad I could help. Remember, it's not impossible to get a loan with a complex income structure. It just takes a bit more effort and creativity.

c55-m1.summary: The user found a house they really like and their offer was accepted.
c55-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Doctor, I have some exciting news. I found a house I really like and my offer was accepted!
Assistant: That's great news! Homeownership can be very fulfilling. How are you feeling about it?
User: I'm feeling a mix of excitement and nerves. It's a big commitment, but I'm ready to take this step.
Assistant: It's completely normal to feel that way. Have you talked to a financial advisor about managing the expenses that come with owning a home?
User: Yes, I have. I've been working out a budget and making sure that my expenses won't exceed my income.
Assistant: That's a good plan. It's important to make sure that you're not financially overextended. How does this new step fit into your long-term goals?
User: It's definitely a step towards my long-term goal of having a stable and secure life. I think owning a home will help me achieve that.
Assistant: That's great to hear. It's important to have goals and take steps to achieve them. It reminds me of when we talked about your desire to improve your physical health and the steps you took towards achieving it.
User: Yes, that's right. I'm still keeping up with my exercise routine and I feel better than ever. It just goes to show that hard work and determination can pay off.
Assistant: Absolutely. I'm proud of you for taking charge of your health and now for taking this exciting new step in your life. Keep up the good work!
User: Mentor, I was looking at housing prices in our city and I was really surprised to see that the average price for a home is $300,000. It seems so high.
Assistant: Yes, housing prices in our city have been on the rise for several years now. It's not just our city, it's a trend across the country.
User: Do you know what's causing the prices to go up so much?
Assistant: There are several factors contributing to the rise in housing prices. One of the main factors is the lack of new housing. There is a shortage of new construction, so demand outstrips supply. This drives prices up.
User: That makes sense. But why are there so few new homes being built?
Assistant: There are a few reasons. One is that there is a shortage of skilled labor in the construction industry. Also, zoning and land use regulations can make it difficult and expensive to build new homes.
User: I see. That's definitely a complex issue.
Assistant: Yes, it is. But there are some things you can do to try and find affordable housing. Have you considered looking at neighborhoods outside of the city center? Home prices tend to be lower in those areas.
User: That's a good suggestion. I'll definitely keep that in mind. Thanks, Mentor.
Assistant: Of course, Mentee. And remember, if you ever have any questions or concerns, don't hesitate to reach out.

User: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: What might be some challenges that borrowers face in obtaining financing amidst the recent surge in demand for new loans?

Passage: When veteran realtor Helen Rowe put a handsome but modest two-bedroom home in West Los Angeles up for sale last month, she figured that the home would sell relatively fast.
Sure, Rowe knew that the real estate market has been in the doldrums: Resales in the Los Angeles area are down 41% from a year ago.
But this home was priced competitively and, in realtorspeak, was in "move-in condition"--immaculate, well-kept and in no need of repairs.
What happened next surprised even Rowe, who has been selling real estate for almost 30 years. The first day, she didn't get a single offer on the property.
Instead, she got six--one of them for the seller's full asking price of $495,000.
"It reminded me of 1987 or '88, when things were so crazy," Rowe said. "I thought the property would sell fast, but I had no idea it would sell this fast."
Across the Southland, there's a growing sentiment among realtors, builders, lenders and other experts that the dormant housing market has snapped out of its 18-month slumber.
They say a combination of factors--a short and successful Gulf War, renewed consumer confidence, lower mortgage rates and bargain-basement home prices--has had buyers coming out in droves since mid-January.
And while few believe that the housing market will soon return to the heady days of '87 and '88, when prices in many areas jumped 20% a year and homes often sold as soon as they were listed, many experts say that the market has bottomed out and is on its way back up.
"I think the train is finally leaving the station," summed up Leslie Appleton-Young, an economist for the California Assn. Of Realtors.
Looking at the statistics provided by the realty trade group, it's hard to make the case that the resale market has finally turned around. Sales are down from Santa Barbara to San Diego, and prices are little changed from a year ago.
But the realty group's figures--which the media uses widely when reporting about the health of the housing market--can be misleading.
That's because they only track transactions that have already been finalized-- they don't reflect deals that have recently been struck but have yet to close escrow.
"All of our members are telling us that business has picked up over the last month or so, and that they're selling more homes," Appleton-Young said. "But those sales won't show up in our statistics for a couple of more months, until all those escrows close and all those keys change hands."
Many realtors think that a lot of keys will soon be changing hands, especially now that the prime spring home-buying season is here.
"I just gave a speech to 200 of our agents, and I asked them, 'How many of you think that the market has bottomed out?' " said Rick Merrill, president of Prudential California Realty.
"Every single one of them raised their hand."
Those agents have good reason for being optimistic: Sales at Prudential's 70 Southland offices in February alone were 50% above January levels. And on the pricey Westside, first-quarter sales are running 70% above the rate posted in the fourth quarter of last year.
"The market just seems to be getting stronger and stronger," Merrill said.
Jon Douglas Co., one of the largest real estate brokerages in the San Fernando Valley and West Side markets, also reports a big upturn in sales.
"We went nine months without having a single $100-million week, but now we've had three in a row," said Jon Douglas, the company's founder.
"I think a lot of the slowness we saw up until January was caused by a 'buyers' rebellion' against the big price increases we saw in '87 and '88," he said. "Now rates are down, the economy is looking better and prices have moderated. The rebellion, I'm happy to say, is over."
Sales are also up at Century 21, whose 500 offices south of Bakersfield make it the Southland's biggest brokerage outfit.
The three regional branches that comprise the bulk of the realty giant's Southern California operations saw nearly 8,500 homes go into escrow last month, up more than 25% from January.
Some C-21 offices are faring even better than others. At Century 21 A Marketplace in Long Beach, broker Phil Jones expects his staffers to sell at least 80 homes this month--twice the amount they sold in February.
"We've got a big bell hanging on the wall that we ring every time one of our agents gets a listing or makes a sale," Jones said. "Lately, it sounds more like we're working in a fire station, not a real estate office."
The sales pace in the San Fernando Valley has also quickened.
Realtors at James R. Gary East Ltd., a big brokerage firm headquartered in Studio City, sold nearly twice as many homes in February as they did a year ago.
"All those people who were sitting on the fence are jumping down and starting to buy," said Temmy Walker, the company's president.
In the San Gabriel Valley community of Arcadia, officials at the local Coldwell Banker office expect their agents to sell between 40 and 50 homes this month--twice the number of homes they sold in March of last year.
"Even the phone calls we're getting have changed," said Marie Murphy, manager of Coldwell's Arcadia branch.
"A few months ago, lots of people were calling and saying, 'I want to sell my home.' Now, most of our callers are saying, 'I want to buy a home.' "
The story is the same in South Orange County and San Diego. Realtors in the San Clemente office of Grubb & Ellis sold 25 homes in all of January: In the first three weeks of March, they sold more than 30.
"Buyers like the low mortgage rates, and they know there are some good deals out there," said Paul Yoder, a Grubb & Ellis district manager. "I hate to use this old cliche, but now is a good time to buy."
The renewed interest among buyers is also good news for home builders, many of whom are coming off one of the worst years for new housing since the 1981-82 recession.
Watt Industries Inc., for example, has long been one of Southern California's biggest builders. But the 2,033 homes it built in 1990 was 20% below its '89 output, and the downturn forced it to lay off hundreds of workers.
But two months ago, sales at its 20 Southland tracts shot up dramatically.
"Back in November or December, we were selling between 13 and 19 homes a week," said Ted Cox, Watt's president. "Then mid-January rolled around, and we started selling 25 or 30 a week. We've been doing gradually better ever since."
Sales have also surged at Kaufman & Broad, another big home builder. In the three-month period that ended Feb. 28, the company sold about 780 homes in the state--a 20% rise from a year ago.
Equally important, the company now has orders for nearly 1,000 homes in California. Just three months ago, its so-called "backlog" was less than 550.
"Everything just seemed to take off in January, when the 'shooting war' started in the Gulf," said Bruce Karatz, Kaufman & Broad's president and chief executive.
"I think the war gave everyone a psychological lift, and it helped a lot of people put their fears about the recession aside. Consumers have got their confidence back, and that's what you need to sell homes."
Builders who cater to the first-time buyers market--generally, homes selling for $150,000 or less in the Inland Empire and $250,000 or less in more urbanized markets such as Orange County--still account for the lion's share of new-home sales.
Van Daele Development, a company that primarily builds homes in the $150,000-range, sold 290 houses in the first 10 weeks of the year--compared to just 81 homes in the previous 10 weeks.
But developers who build more expensive houses for "trade-up" buyers say they're enjoying a big upswing in sales too.
"The 'trade-up' market has gotten a boost because the resale market has finally picked up," said Eric Brown of the Meyers Group, an Encino-based real estate research and consulting group.
"It's a pretty simple equation: You can't buy a more expensive home if you can't sell the one you already own. Now that the resale market is doing better, people are looking at nicer, new homes again."
Prices for new homes have dropped in many parts of the Southland over the last year, and have remained stagnant in most others. But that too could soon change, as inventory shrinks and new houses become harder to find.
For example, the number of new homes for sale in Orange County and the booming Palmdale/Lancaster area of northern Los Angeles County have dropped between 20% and 30% over the last three months, according to the Meyers Group's statistics.
Inventory is down about 10% in San Bernardino and 5% in San Diego County.
"We'll keep seeing those inventory levels decline as the year progresses, and that will eventually put upward pressure on prices," Brown said.
The dwindling backlog of new homes has allowed many builders to drop or scale back costly sales incentives that they were using to lure would-be buyers only a few months ago.
For example, just last winter Watt Industries had 450 homes sitting empty at its Southland housing tracts. To spur sales, it was common for Watt to offer $10,000 in free upgrades--from better carpeting to nicer cabinets--to its prospective buyers.
Now Watt has only about 280 homes for sale, and it's hard to get an upgrade package worth more than $5,000 at many of its projects.
"I think you'll see most of the incentives disappear relatively soon, and you'll see some across-the-board price increases by summertime," said Watt's Cox.
Already, some buyers seem to sense that the market has bottomed out--and that waiting could prove to be expensive.
Twice this month, the Fieldstone Co. Opened two new phases in the master-planned community of Rancho Santa Margarita. And both times, dozens of people literally camped outside the development's sales office for up to two weeks in the hope of being able to plunk down as much as $292,000 to buy a home of their own.
"Buyers are seeing some tremendous new-home values now, and they're smart enough to know that they aren't going to last forever," said Frank Foster, a Fieldstone executive.
One key factor behind the recent upturn in sales is the downward trend in mortgage rates.
Rates on 30-year, fixed-rate loans now stand at about 9 1/2%, down from a peak of nearly 11% last year. The 1 1/2-point drop has knocked $140 off the monthly payments on a $125,000 loan.
Most banks and savings and loan associations were already enjoying a big upswing in business, as homeowners rushed to refinance their mortgages at the new, lower rates. Now, their profits are being fattened by all the buyers looking for loans to finance their purchases.
"Our business over the past four weeks is up more than 50% from the same period a year ago," said Howard Levine, president of ARCS Mortgage in Calabasas. "Borrowers are coming out of the woodwork."
Added Dallas Brewer, executive vice president of lending giant Home Savings of America: "We've got between 9,000 and 10,000 loans being processed right now. At Christmastime, we only had about 4,500 in the pipeline."
While today's lower mortgage rates are a blessing for borrowers, the news isn't all good.
Recent regulatory changes brought about by the S&L; crisis have forced many lenders to tighten their loan requirements and demand bigger down payments, making it tougher for some borrowers to get financing.
And because of the prolonged housing slump, some lenders were forced to cut their staffs by as much as 50%. Now, some experts say, bankers may have a tough time coping if they continue to be deluged with new loan applications.
"The bottom line is, it might take a lot longer to get your loan processed and close your deal," said Barry Havemann, president of HSH Associates, a lending-research firm based in New Jersey.
Most big lenders, however, say they won't have any trouble coping with a prolonged deluge of loan requests.
"Most of us have become so automated and streamlined that we can handle virtually any level of business without any strain," said Sam Lyons, senior vice president of Great Western Bank.

"All of our members are telling us that business has picked up over the last month or so, and that they're selling more homes," Appleton-Young said. "But those sales won't show up in our statistics for a couple of more months, until all those escrows close and all those keys change hands."

"The market just seems to be getting stronger and stronger," Merrill said.
Jon Douglas Co., one of the largest real estate brokerages in the San Fernando Valley and West Side markets, also reports a big upturn in sales.

Passage: When veteran realtor Helen Rowe put a handsome but modest two-bedroom home in West Los Angeles up for sale last month, she figured that the home would sell relatively fast.
Sure, Rowe knew that the real estate market has been in the doldrums: Resales in the Los Angeles area are down 41% from a year ago.
But this home was priced competitively and, in realtorspeak, was in "move-in condition"--immaculate, well-kept and in no need of repairs.
What happened next surprised even Rowe, who has been selling real estate for almost 30 years. The first day, she didn't get a single offer on the property.
Instead, she got six--one of them for the seller's full asking price of $495,000.
"It reminded me of 1987 or '88, when things were so crazy," Rowe said. "I thought the property would sell fast, but I had no idea it would sell this fast."
Across the Southland, there's a growing sentiment among realtors, builders, lenders and other experts that the dormant housing market has snapped out of its 18-month slumber.
They say a combination of factors--a short and successful Gulf War, renewed consumer confidence, lower mortgage rates and bargain-basement home prices--has had buyers coming out in droves since mid-January.
And while few believe that the housing market will soon return to the heady days of '87 and '88, when prices in many areas jumped 20% a year and homes often sold as soon as they were listed, many experts say that the market has bottomed out and is on its way back up.
"I think the train is finally leaving the station," summed up Leslie Appleton-Young, an economist for the California Assn. Of Realtors.
Looking at the statistics provided by the realty trade group, it's hard to make the case that the resale market has finally turned around. Sales are down from Santa Barbara to San Diego, and prices are little changed from a year ago.
But the realty group's figures--which the media uses widely when reporting about the health of the housing market--can be misleading.
That's because they only track transactions that have already been finalized-- they don't reflect deals that have recently been struck but have yet to close escrow.
"All of our members are telling us that business has picked up over the last month or so, and that they're selling more homes," Appleton-Young said. "But those sales won't show up in our statistics for a couple of more months, until all those escrows close and all those keys change hands."
Many realtors think that a lot of keys will soon be changing hands, especially now that the prime spring home-buying season is here.
"I just gave a speech to 200 of our agents, and I asked them, 'How many of you think that the market has bottomed out?' " said Rick Merrill, president of Prudential California Realty.
"Every single one of them raised their hand."
Those agents have good reason for being optimistic: Sales at Prudential's 70 Southland offices in February alone were 50% above January levels. And on the pricey Westside, first-quarter sales are running 70% above the rate posted in the fourth quarter of last year.
"The market just seems to be getting stronger and stronger," Merrill said.
Jon Douglas Co., one of the largest real estate brokerages in the San Fernando Valley and West Side markets, also reports a big upturn in sales.
"We went nine months without having a single $100-million week, but now we've had three in a row," said Jon Douglas, the company's founder.
"I think a lot of the slowness we saw up until January was caused by a 'buyers' rebellion' against the big price increases we saw in '87 and '88," he said. "Now rates are down, the economy is looking better and prices have moderated. The rebellion, I'm happy to say, is over."
Sales are also up at Century 21, whose 500 offices south of Bakersfield make it the Southland's biggest brokerage outfit.
The three regional branches that comprise the bulk of the realty giant's Southern California operations saw nearly 8,500 homes go into escrow last month, up more than 25% from January.
Some C-21 offices are faring even better than others. At Century 21 A Marketplace in Long Beach, broker Phil Jones expects his staffers to sell at least 80 homes this month--twice the amount they sold in February.
"We've got a big bell hanging on the wall that we ring every time one of our agents gets a listing or makes a sale," Jones said. "Lately, it sounds more like we're working in a fire station, not a real estate office."
The sales pace in the San Fernando Valley has also quickened.
Realtors at James R. Gary East Ltd., a big brokerage firm headquartered in Studio City, sold nearly twice as many homes in February as they did a year ago.
"All those people who were sitting on the fence are jumping down and starting to buy," said Temmy Walker, the company's president.
In the San Gabriel Valley community of Arcadia, officials at the local Coldwell Banker office expect their agents to sell between 40 and 50 homes this month--twice the number of homes they sold in March of last year.
"Even the phone calls we're getting have changed," said Marie Murphy, manager of Coldwell's Arcadia branch.
"A few months ago, lots of people were calling and saying, 'I want to sell my home.' Now, most of our callers are saying, 'I want to buy a home.' "
The story is the same in South Orange County and San Diego. Realtors in the San Clemente office of Grubb & Ellis sold 25 homes in all of January: In the first three weeks of March, they sold more than 30.
"Buyers like the low mortgage rates, and they know there are some good deals out there," said Paul Yoder, a Grubb & Ellis district manager. "I hate to use this old cliche, but now is a good time to buy."
The renewed interest among buyers is also good news for home builders, many of whom are coming off one of the worst years for new housing since the 1981-82 recession.
Watt Industries Inc., for example, has long been one of Southern California's biggest builders. But the 2,033 homes it built in 1990 was 20% below its '89 output, and the downturn forced it to lay off hundreds of workers.
But two months ago, sales at its 20 Southland tracts shot up dramatically.
"Back in November or December, we were selling between 13 and 19 homes a week," said Ted Cox, Watt's president. "Then mid-January rolled around, and we started selling 25 or 30 a week. We've been doing gradually better ever since."
Sales have also surged at Kaufman & Broad, another big home builder. In the three-month period that ended Feb. 28, the company sold about 780 homes in the state--a 20% rise from a year ago.
Equally important, the company now has orders for nearly 1,000 homes in California. Just three months ago, its so-called "backlog" was less than 550.
"Everything just seemed to take off in January, when the 'shooting war' started in the Gulf," said Bruce Karatz, Kaufman & Broad's president and chief executive.
"I think the war gave everyone a psychological lift, and it helped a lot of people put their fears about the recession aside. Consumers have got their confidence back, and that's what you need to sell homes."
Builders who cater to the first-time buyers market--generally, homes selling for $150,000 or less in the Inland Empire and $250,000 or less in more urbanized markets such as Orange County--still account for the lion's share of new-home sales.
Van Daele Development, a company that primarily builds homes in the $150,000-range, sold 290 houses in the first 10 weeks of the year--compared to just 81 homes in the previous 10 weeks.
But developers who build more expensive houses for "trade-up" buyers say they're enjoying a big upswing in sales too.
"The 'trade-up' market has gotten a boost because the resale market has finally picked up," said Eric Brown of the Meyers Group, an Encino-based real estate research and consulting group.
"It's a pretty simple equation: You can't buy a more expensive home if you can't sell the one you already own. Now that the resale market is doing better, people are looking at nicer, new homes again."
Prices for new homes have dropped in many parts of the Southland over the last year, and have remained stagnant in most others. But that too could soon change, as inventory shrinks and new houses become harder to find.
For example, the number of new homes for sale in Orange County and the booming Palmdale/Lancaster area of northern Los Angeles County have dropped between 20% and 30% over the last three months, according to the Meyers Group's statistics.
Inventory is down about 10% in San Bernardino and 5% in San Diego County.
"We'll keep seeing those inventory levels decline as the year progresses, and that will eventually put upward pressure on prices," Brown said.
The dwindling backlog of new homes has allowed many builders to drop or scale back costly sales incentives that they were using to lure would-be buyers only a few months ago.
For example, just last winter Watt Industries had 450 homes sitting empty at its Southland housing tracts. To spur sales, it was common for Watt to offer $10,000 in free upgrades--from better carpeting to nicer cabinets--to its prospective buyers.
Now Watt has only about 280 homes for sale, and it's hard to get an upgrade package worth more than $5,000 at many of its projects.
"I think you'll see most of the incentives disappear relatively soon, and you'll see some across-the-board price increases by summertime," said Watt's Cox.
Already, some buyers seem to sense that the market has bottomed out--and that waiting could prove to be expensive.
Twice this month, the Fieldstone Co. Opened two new phases in the master-planned community of Rancho Santa Margarita. And both times, dozens of people literally camped outside the development's sales office for up to two weeks in the hope of being able to plunk down as much as $292,000 to buy a home of their own.
"Buyers are seeing some tremendous new-home values now, and they're smart enough to know that they aren't going to last forever," said Frank Foster, a Fieldstone executive.
One key factor behind the recent upturn in sales is the downward trend in mortgage rates.
Rates on 30-year, fixed-rate loans now stand at about 9 1/2%, down from a peak of nearly 11% last year. The 1 1/2-point drop has knocked $140 off the monthly payments on a $125,000 loan.
Most banks and savings and loan associations were already enjoying a big upswing in business, as homeowners rushed to refinance their mortgages at the new, lower rates. Now, their profits are being fattened by all the buyers looking for loans to finance their purchases.
"Our business over the past four weeks is up more than 50% from the same period a year ago," said Howard Levine, president of ARCS Mortgage in Calabasas. "Borrowers are coming out of the woodwork."
Added Dallas Brewer, executive vice president of lending giant Home Savings of America: "We've got between 9,000 and 10,000 loans being processed right now. At Christmastime, we only had about 4,500 in the pipeline."
While today's lower mortgage rates are a blessing for borrowers, the news isn't all good.
Recent regulatory changes brought about by the S&L; crisis have forced many lenders to tighten their loan requirements and demand bigger down payments, making it tougher for some borrowers to get financing.
And because of the prolonged housing slump, some lenders were forced to cut their staffs by as much as 50%. Now, some experts say, bankers may have a tough time coping if they continue to be deluged with new loan applications.
"The bottom line is, it might take a lot longer to get your loan processed and close your deal," said Barry Havemann, president of HSH Associates, a lending-research firm based in New Jersey.
Most big lenders, however, say they won't have any trouble coping with a prolonged deluge of loan requests.
"Most of us have become so automated and streamlined that we can handle virtually any level of business without any strain," said Sam Lyons, senior vice president of Great Western Bank.

Question/Instruction: What is the key to stabilizing the housing market, according to the text material?

Given material: The trick will be for rates to move higher in an orderly and not-too-rapid pace.
The question is not whether higher interest rates are good or bad right now but rather: How much higher should they be?
Interest rates are the heartbeat of the economy and since the beginning of the financial crisis it has been easy to see why the unusually low rates were appropriate. We witnessed the economy come to its knees and markets around the world plunge into fear and panic unlike we have seen in decades. Now more than three years later, as we sift through the aftermath, it is clear to me that instead of potentially derailing the recovery, as we hear so much about, higher interest rates will be the key to success.
During ordinary cycles the first hint of higher rates and possible Fed tightening will cause shudders to ripple through the markets with the warning of tougher times to come. But don’t flinch.
The key to the recovery is the stabilization of the housing market. Investors that are considering a move into real estate have no incentive to move off the sidelines. With the Fed on hold and signaling to the markets their intent to keep rates low, investors are comfortable in “wait and see” mode believing that they will still have access to low rates for a long time to come. If long rates begin to drift up I believe it will move some people off the sidelines which will begin to move the needle on housing prices.
As housing prices stabilize and begin to move positively, this will provide a two-fold benefit to the economy. Homeowners would gain a greater sense of confidence, positively influencing their willingness to spend. Banks would have a greater incentive with higher rates and gain some comfort in lending more which would stimulate the flow of liquidity sitting as excess capital in banks today. This could go a long way to driving economic activity and stimulating the need to hire!
The trick will be for rates to move higher in an orderly and not-too-rapid pace. But make no mistake – higher they must go, and soon.
